If you're ever feeling down about life, a single night with a blanket and Spirited Away can lift you up. I call them "movies for the soul". 

The Intouchables might be what you need. Reconnecting with life, finding meaning when you're lost, etc. 

For films more like what you're talking about (overcoming a mid-life or quarter-life crisis), I can think of American Beauty, The Secret Life of Walter Mitty, Lost in Translation, Falling Down, Into the Wild, Her, and Good Will Hunting.

not like Ikiru but Trees Lounge is a drama/comedy about a middle age loser still living in his hometown. Somehow both uplifting and a depressing cautionary tale. might jolt you out of a slump

>Are you looking for a film that inspires you in spite of these feelings, or one to simply find solace in due to being relatable?

This was the Q I was wondering as well. But for whatever reason, these films come to mind:

* Tampopo (1985, Dir. Juzo Itami)
* The Taste of Tea (2004, Dir. Katsuhito Ishii)
* Children of Men (2006, Dir. Alfonso Cuarón)
* Michael Clayton (2007, Dir. Tony Gilroy)

Definitely one that helps inspire me! 

I've always believed that the most human thing one can do is to simply like something.

For me, I've struggled a lot with balancing my life the way I want, and the way society expects. I want to pursue things that likely won't be viable, and every day I find myself shoved more and more into a corner where I should just choose a path that makes the most money. 

Kanji Watanabe lived in a world that was not always the most receptive to his own personal memories and experiences. In building the playground, Watanabe also chose a path which may have not even succeeded at all. But it wouldn't have mattered, because at least he can say that he placed unwavering certainty into something he sincerely cared about. 

At one point in my life, like Watanabe I hope that I can place that same sort of faith into a personal achievement that no one around me can take away from me.

Watch Stalker by Andre Tarkovsky, it’s in hbo max. In all seriousness you won’t feel like you do now after you watch it. You may look at yourself, and your desires and perceived failures in a profoundly different way

In so far as a film operates under an artistic representation of catharsis, which I think is a major part of the appeal of Ikiru (a Great GREAT film) another Japanese movie which really stuck with me was After Life (1998).

I think part of worrying about significance is not understanding the grand insignificance of everything. You think you failed but everyone does. It's understanding one's failures that mean anything - give true perspective. So, yeah. After Life .... or just feel weird and bad and dive into that, watch vonTrier's The House that Jack Built, watch your skin crawl off.

Bold move to suggest someone who is borderline depressed watch a Tarkovsky.

But who knows, It just might work.

You should check out Good Morning. Boys fight with their parents to get a TV set. In one scene, a man farts and it's mistaken for speech. Ozu's films are wistful, so if you like this you'd probably like his other films.


One of the last films I saw with my mother is Harold and Maude. A morose young man meets an elderly lady who teaches him how to live. My mother was significantly older and had an indomitable spirit like Maude's. 


+ It's a Wonderful Life

Forrest Gump - a blockbuster that doesn't need more introduction, but the way he touched so many people's lives wherever he goes, sometimes just simply by running, was heartwarming. Full of american historical events and tidbits, and fantastic cinematic too.

About a Boy - a smaller, more obscure move compared to Forrest Gump, and more grounded and realistic in a way. It's a story about a 30-something low-tier trust fund baby (Hugh Grant) who never had to work in his entire life (his late dad wrote a famous Christmas jingle and he inherited the wealth and the non-stop annual stream of royalties) who spent his time womanizing and watching TV all day long. His life changed when a boy of a single mom befriended him by accident, and he in turn tried to use the friendship to hit on another single mom (Rachel Weisz). Wholesome ending with great character development, and fantastic soundtrack too.
My friends wanted to watch Stalker with me and they were confused. I do think it’s very hit or miss. I’m naturally a snob-head, so I got what it was trying to say… I think

Depends on what type of failure. The general answer would be something like the Shawshank Redemption. Maybe you’ve already seen it, though. 

My go-to-feel good movie has always been thr Truman Show. Just a man literally fighting against all the odds in order to achieve some sort of meaning. I’m making it sound sappy, but the ending never ceases to make me smile.

Two of my favourite movies fit this feeling well. *Andrei Rublev*, directed by Tarkovski, is a slow cinema masterpiece about the icon painter Andrei Rublev and his crisis of faith that leaves him unable to create his art.

The other is *An Elephant Sitting Still,* which follows a group of dissimilar characters living in urban Northern China, all of whom have (to some degree) abandoned their notions of living a good life, and only hold out hope for the possibility of seeing a circus elephant which has been abused into never moving from its spot.

Jeff, Who Lives at Home may fit the bill for what you are looking for. It is about a man who, well, is living at home (I’m sure you could guess his name too). He is lost in life and looking for signs all around him trying to find meaning and inspiration. It stars Jason Segel and Ed Helms. It’s a dark comedy, pretty short to boot as well. I am not sure which platform it is streaming on, if any.

I am thinking of ending things (2020) by Charlie Kaufman for sure .

"It's not bad, once you stop feeling sorry for yourself because you're just a pig, or, even worse, a pig infested with maggots. Someone has to be a pig infested with maggots, right? It might as well be you. It's the luck of the draw."
One of the most devastating dialogue I'd ever heard
*Nostalghia* - a tale of two guys trying to light a match. And then there's *The Sacrifice* finale...

Good film, but one of his "bad" trilogy, Knight of Cups fits what OP wants. The film is like a gentle meditation for people who are lull to their present life and aimless in their life. Maybe OP will find the film suits their current emotional states.

Frances Ha is a very interesting film about a character that seems lost and without a purpose. It stars Greta Gerwig, who also co-wrote it with her director and partner Noah Baumbach. IMO, to this day, that's her best film, and his best film. I remember the hype around Lady Bird, which I nicknamed "CW's Frances Ha", because it doesn't even come close to the impact of that movie.

If you like Ikiru and Kurosawa, I’d definitely check out One Wonderful Sunday (1947).  It’s one of his earlier movies about a dead broke couple living in the devastated post-war Japan. I know that a somewhat romantic movie might not be what you’re looking for, but I honestly didn’t see it as that.  It really dives into perspective and how world outlook can deeply affect your emotions. It’s a story about resilience, hope, and appreciation. Ikiru is a great, emotional experience, but there’s something in One Wonderful Sunday that hit me on a different level. 

I hope you’re able to get something from this. Stay strong, we’re rooting for you.

I would recommend Wim Wenders’ Wings of Desire. If I could describe it in a sentence, it is a meditation on humanity and our connection to each other. 

It’s a film with some potentially difficult themes, but I think overall provides a really understated, yet powerful message that touches on some of things you reference in your OP.

A bunch of good recommendations in the comments already. Let me add a couple of personal favs:  
  
Postmen in the Mountains (1999)  
Fish Story (2009)  
Pusher 2 (2004; might be less impactful without having seen the first)  
**Eureka (2000; Shinji Aoyama)**  
Bright Future (2003; Kiyoshi Kurosawa)  
A Scene at the Sea (1991)

You may also want to check out whatever seems appealing to you by Hirokazu Kore'eda as well as Ryusuke Hamaguchi, with the latter probably being more emotionally complex and less accessible.
